Made me laugh:

A Frenchman, an Englishman, and a German were each commissioned to conduct a study of the camel.

The Frenchman went to the Jardin des Plantes, spent half an hour there, questioned the keeper, threw some bread to the camel, teased it with the tip of his umbrella, and then went home and wrote, for his newspaper, a lively column full of witty and incisive observations.

The Englishman, taking along his tea basket and a comfortable set of camping equipment, went off to pitch his tent in the lands of the East. As for the German, full of contempt for the Frenchman’s frivolity and the Englishman’s lack of general ideas, he shut himself up in his room to write a work in several volumes entitled: The Idea of the Camel Derived from the Conception of the Self.

Basically, ESMA wants crypto platforms to take more responsibility for the services they offer you.

Here’s what that could look like:

→ You stake through an exchange: it should tell you what it charges, how long your tokens are locked, and how you could lose money.

→ You lend crypto to earn interest: the platform should explain where your coins go and what could go wrong.

→ An app connects you to DeFi: the company behind it could have to check the protocols it offers and explain the risks, even when smart contracts handle the transactions.

→ A company calls itself decentralized: regulators want to look at who actually controls it before deciding whether it qualifies for an exemption.

Whether this is good for crypto depends on who ends up covered by the rules and what they’re expected to do.

For now, it’s still a proposal.

It might seem like people in tech and investing have lost their minds. And in some sense that is true. But a lot of the behavior is rational in some sense, even if it’s not “honorable” 

Why is it happening now? Yes, some people have AI psychosis. But something deeper is happening 

In life, there are two types of games. Single turn and multi turn games. Single turn, or one-shot, games are just what they sound like. One turn and the game is over. No more turns. 

Multi turn, or sequential, games have multiple turns. Which means history, reputation, and consequences for your actions have a large impact. You expect to see the players on the board multiple times in the future 

Most things in the game of life are multi turn. Careers are long. Investments take time to come to fruition, and you will want to redeploy the capital 

But when the stakes get high enough, people start to squint at the board and see that they can end the game in one turn. Or at least they think they can. 

I’ve talked a lot about how AI is the big one. So it’s not crazy to me that some people are looking at the board and thinking there might be only one turn left, and they are just going for it.

After 3 years building LLM agents, I think the model people actually choose to run says a lot, it’s a bit like voting with your credit card. That’s why the benchmark I pay the most attention to is usage on OpenRouter.

For smaller/cheaper models, DeepSeek Flash is doing ~22.7T tokens a week, GLM Flash ~10.6T and GPT-6 Luna ~5.1T, which gives you a pretty good idea of where people are finding value for money.

For larger, frontier models, Opus 5.5 is at ~1.9T and GPT-6 Sol ~1.2T, while Gemini Pro is at ~0.2T, roughly 10x less volume than Opus.

Obviously cheaper models will consume more tokens, so you have to compare within each category, but I find this much more useful than another benchmark showing a model winning by 2 points. You can game a benchmark but not where companies are spending their $$$.

And that still only gives you the global trend. For your product, the eval that matters is your own, on actual customer tasks, because a model can be amazing overall and still suck at the specific thing you need it to do.

That’s why I think you want a multi-model platform, with customer evals driving which model handles which task, so you can improve quality and optimize your token stack as the models change. You shouldn’t be married to one model.
